Three things stacked up: (1) Alphabet raised FY26 capex guidance to $195-205B from $180-190B, spooking margin-watchers; (2) the Sep 18 AI-antitrust lawsuit overhang is still live; (3) Meta's "Muse" assistant (bypasses Google's ad-supported surfaces inside Gmail/Docs/Calendar) is being read as a fresh competitive threat. Nothing here changes the halal read (core business still search/ads/cloud), but it explains why price is sitting inside the 2% WATCH band on the stop.

🟢 SPXC — Completed the $410M FIS Water acquisition Sep 15 (HVAC/water side, unrelated to the Kranze defense segment that drives the exit call) and picked up an Outperform initiation at Wolfe Research the same day — neither changes the exit decision. The bigger move: Nvidia's warm-water-cooling keynote comments triggered a sector-wide selloff in air-cooling names (SPXC, Trane, Modine, Johnson Controls, Carrier), dragging SPXC from above $230 to a fresh 52-week low near $172.55 this week. TD Cowen argues the market overreacted (towers complement liquid cooling, not compete with it) and SPXC just raised its data-center capacity target to $1.1B — but none of that matters for the halal-driven exit already in motion.

📚 Today you learned

Margin Guidance Ranges — Why Foundries Guide in Bands, Not Points

TSM just guided Q3 gross margin at 65-67% — a 2-point band, not a single number. That's not hedging for its own sake. Foundry margins move with node mix (how much revenue comes from bleeding-edge 3nm/2nm vs. mature nodes), yield (new nodes start ~50% and climb over quarters), and utilization, all of which shift week to week as customers pull orders forward or back. A 2-point band on a $45B quarter is ±$900M of gross profit — real money, not rounding. When you see a company guide a range instead of a point estimate, the width of that range tells you how much visibility management actually has: TSM's 2-point band signals confidence; a newer fabless company might guide ±5-8 points because it genuinely doesn't know. Read the width, not just the midpoint.

Also today: Node mix — the % of a foundry's revenue coming from its newest, highest-margin process nodes vs. older, cheaper ones; rising mix is a margin tailwind even at flat pricing.
